newsitem.title: NEPAL: Nepal vote delayed, opposition stages sit-in.
newsitem.headline: Nepal vote delayed, opposition stages sit-in.

text.p: Nepal's parliament will reconvene on Tuesday after the opposition disrupted a no-confidence motion against the government, alleging the ruling coalition had forcibly kept away its supporters.

Confusion reigned in the Himalayan kingdom for several hours during a debate on Prime Minister Sher Bahadur Deuba's 15-month-old centre-right coalition, after communists complained that some of their key supporters had vanished.

At one stage on Monday night almost the entire opposition staged a sit-in in the central aisle of parliament and snatched away the microphone from the speaker to stop efforts to push through the vote, witnesses said.
Speaker Ram Chandra Poudel finally adjourned the lower house for a third time in the late night session and said it would reconvene at one p.m. (0715 GMT) on Tuesday.

The opposition said five government ministers and one deputy each from two minor parties, the Nepal Workers and Peasants Party (NWPP) and the Nepal Sadbhavana Party (NSP), were kept away by the government for fear that they would vote against it.

"Without a minister's reply about the information on the missing ministers and the members, the business of the house cannot proceed," said Khadga Prasad Oli, deputy of the main opposition Unified Marxist Leninist (UML) party.
Prime Minister Deuba is to reply before the vote can be carried out.

The NWPP announced earlier in the day that its three deputies would vote against the government. The chief of the NSP is a member of the government, but two remaining deputies of his party had said they would vote against the coalition.
"One of my three deputies is missing since the morning from his residence," said NWPP's president, Narayan Man Bijukuchhe.

"Five ministers were sent to Bangkok for fear that they will vote against the government," said former minister Kamal Thapa of the Rashtriya Prajatantra Party (RPP), who resigned from the coalition last week to campaign against the government.
Deuba denied any wrongdoing and said the ministers had gone to Bangkok for medical treatment.
"No one has been kidnapped and I am ready to retire from politics if it is proved that the government has kidnapped anyone," he told parliament.
"I have authorised the ministers to go to Bangkok for medical treatment."
Constituents of the coalition are divided over support for the government.
NWPP's support for the no-confidence motion, moved on Saturday by the UML, had increased the chances that the government would lose a close-run vote, politicians said.
Deuba's three-party coalition commands 108 seats in a house of 205 members. Of this, Deuba's Nepali Congress has 86 members and the RPP 19. But the RPP is sharply divided.
Politicians estimated that the decision by NWPP will raise the number of votes in support of the motion to 104, just above the 103 required to pass it.

Deuba's Nepali Congress was demanding disqualification of the two defecting NSP members. If it succeeded the opposition will lose two crucial votes. But one of the two NSP members was not present in the house, and this sparked protests.
